title: SYSK Selects: Do you stay conscious after being decapitated?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode on whether a person stays conscious after decapitation. Josh introduces it as one of the grizzliest episodes. The hosts open with banter about dreams, neural networks, Francis Crick's "astonishing hypothesis," and EEG brain-wave measurement of consciousness. They discuss a Dutch study (Radboud University, Netherlands) where rats were decapitated while attached to EEGs; brain activity persisted about four seconds, with a final burst around fifty seconds later. They cover the history of beheading (Judith and Holofernes, Roman practice, Saudi Arabia's trained headsmen, sword and axe executions), the guillotine (credited to Joseph-Ignace Guillotin as its champion, invented by Antoine Louis, used in the Reign of Terror, last French execution in 1977), Charlotte Corday being slapped by an executioner, and anecdotal accounts: Charles I and Strafford, Lavoisier blinking, Languille's eye focusing when called by Dr. Beaurieux, and Mike the headless chicken. Closing segments include a listener poem from Alex, calls for pet stories, and site promotion.

segments.title: Selects intro and morning banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode as one of the grizzliest selections and warns listeners. Chuck and Josh chat about birds, sleep, and a dream about renting a car.

segments.title: Dreams, neurons, and the astonishing hypothesis
segments.summary: The hosts discuss dream theory, Francis Crick's astonishing hypothesis that thoughts and experiences are neuron activity, and how EEG measures brain electrical activity as a sign of consciousness.

segments.title: Dutch rat decapitation study
segments.summary: Researchers at Radboud University in the Netherlands attached rats to EEGs and decapitated them. Brain electrical activity continued for about four seconds, then stopped, with one final burst around fifty seconds later.

segments.title: History of beheading and capital punishment
segments.summary: The hosts trace beheading from the Judith and Holofernes story and Roman practice to modern Saudi Arabia, where trained headsmen use swords. They note that earlier executions with knives, axes, or swords often took several blows.

segments.title: The guillotine and the Reign of Terror
segments.summary: The guillotine was invented by Antoine Louis and promoted by Joseph-Ignace Guillotin as humane. Its use grew during the Reign of Terror. The hosts describe its mechanism, the shield and basket, and France's use of it until 1977.

segments.title: Anecdotes of consciousness after decapitation
segments.summary: The hosts recount Charlotte Corday being slapped by an executioner, reports of Charles I and others moving lips and eyes, Lavoisier's reported blinking, Languille's eyes focusing when called, a German physician's pain reaction from spinal probing, and Mike the headless chicken. They conclude that the answer is yes, at least for several seconds.

segments.title: Listener poem and sign-off
segments.summary: Josh reads a birthday poem from listener Alex, promotes the site search, and asks listeners to send unusual pet stories. The show closes with app and site plugs.
